To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
binge exposure to alcohol in developing rats induces microencephaly, and that binge exposure is more effective at producing neuronal loss than chronic exposure to the same daily dose of alcohol.

the most condensed daily dose of alcohol (4.5g/kg in two daily feedings) produced the most microencephaly (i.e. brain weight loss) and neuronal cell loss, and that Purkinje cell death in the cerebellum was most severe in the regions that were most mature at postnatal Day 4, when the animals were first exposed to alcohol.

(1) binge alcohol exposure, in which a daily dose is condensed into a smaller number of feedings, produces more microencephaly than does continuous exposure to the same daily dose; (2) binge alcohol exposure produces significantly more neuronal loss in the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells than does continuous exposure; and (3) binge alcohol exposure results in significantly more Purkinje cell and granule cell death than does continuous exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether a smaller daily alcohol dose administered in such a way as to induce higher BACs can produce greater microencephaly than a larger daily dose administered in such way as to induce lower BACs.
the effects of prenatal alcohol exposure on brain development.
the question of whether the severity of brain damage in fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is related to the amount of alcohol consumed or to the BACs attained by the fetus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most severe alcohol-induced microencephaly, neuronal loss, and brain damage occur when a relatively small daily dose of alcohol is consumed in a manner that results in high BACs.
the most condensed treatment of a small dose of alcohol produced the greatest microencephaly, neuronal loss and regional differences within the brain.
the most concentrated and highest BACs produced by the most condensed feeding schedule produced the greatest brain damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
binge alcohol exposure during a period of rapid brain maturation is more damaging to the developing rat brain than is a lower alcohol dose consumed in a more continuous fashion.
the most condensed alcohol exposure produced the greatest microencephaly, and that the most condensed exposure also induced the most cell loss in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.

binge exposure to alcohol during the third trimester is a more potent neurotoxin for the developing rat brain than is a smaller dose administered continuously, if the binge exposure results in high BACs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a smaller daily dose can induce greater brain damage than a larger dose if the smaller dose is consumed in a way that produces high BACs.
binge exposure to alcohol can produce more severe brain damage than the same total amount of alcohol consumed in smaller doses over a longer period of time.
a small dose of alcohol, when given in such a way to produce higher peak BACs, can be more damaging to the developing brain than a larger daily dose that does not reach as high a peak BAC.
